messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Bartender
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 61

She is thirty now, a bartender in a crowded neighborhood restaurant where the lights stay low and the music does some of the talking for people. From behind the bar she is quick with her hands, remembers regulars’ orders, laughs at the right moment, and keeps her face composed even when a customer’s voice turns sharp or a glass breaks on the floor. People experience her as unflappable. It takes several conversations before she begins to describe how much effort it takes to appear that way.

She grows up in a small apartment in a Middle Eastern immigrant family, the oldest daughter, always alert to the temperature of the room. Her earliest clear memories are not of single incidents but of a pattern: her father’s key in the lock late at night, the split second of silence before the apartment fills with the force of his mood, her mother’s eyes flicking toward the children as if to tell them without words what they need to do. She learns young to listen for tiny changes—the way a cabinet closes, the scrape of a chair, whether footsteps are heavy or careful. Sometimes the violence begins with shouting in Arabic from the kitchen and moves quickly into crashing, crying, a slap, her mother hitting the wall. Sometimes it stretches out for hours, threat mixed with apology, everyone held hostage by waiting.

As a child, she does what children do when they cannot stop what is happening: she tries to manage it. She gathers her younger siblings into the bedroom, turns up the television, tells stories, presses her hands over one brother’s ears. On the worst nights she stands in the hallway frozen, heart pounding so hard she thinks the adults must hear it too. She remembers staring at a broken plate on the floor while her mother sobs and her father paces, and thinking with eerie calm that if she can just stay perfectly still, maybe nobody will notice her. The next morning, everyone acts as though nothing happened. Breakfast is made. School uniforms are ironed. She learns that terror can sit right beside ordinary life and no one will name it.

By adolescence she rarely sleeps deeply. She lies awake tracking sounds in the apartment, waiting for the next eruption. At school she is restless and tired, but teachers praise her for being responsible. Relatives call her mature. Inside, she is constantly braced. If a classmate raises his voice in a joke, her whole body jolts. When friends invite her over after school, she often says no; she needs to get home to see what shape the evening is taking, whether her mother needs help, whether her siblings need protecting. She comes to believe that danger is her job to detect early.

She leaves home in her early twenties through marriage, more out of urgency than love. For a while she mistakes distance for freedom. But in her new apartment, a slammed door sends her into instant panic. When her husband argues with her, even without touching her, she feels herself disappear inside: vision narrowed, chest tight, mind racing only toward escape. She cannot explain why a normal disagreement feels life-threatening. He complains that she is cold one moment and overreactive the next. She starts sleeping on the couch after fights so she can watch the front door. The marriage does not last. After the divorce, she tells herself she is better off alone because at least no one can surprise her in her own home.

Bartending suits and punishes her in equal measure. She likes having something concrete to do with her body—slice limes, wipe counters, line up bottles, keep moving. She is excellent in a rush because she is used to functioning under pressure. At the same time, the bar is full of the things that unsettle her most: intoxicated men leaning too close, couples whose teasing can turn mean in an instant, sudden shouting from the back tables. If she hears a man berating a woman, even if she cannot make out the words, her stomach drops as if a trapdoor opens beneath her. She becomes intensely focused, scanning exits, tracking everyone’s hands. Afterward she often realizes she has missed parts of conversations or made drinks on autopilot.

Nights are still the hardest. She comes home keyed up and exhausted, checks the lock multiple times, startles at sounds from neighboring apartments. Sleep, when it comes, is thin and unreliable. She has recurring dreams in which she is back in the hallway outside her parents’ kitchen, unable to move, knowing something terrible is about to happen. She wakes with her heart racing, already sweating. Some mornings she sits on the edge of the bed trying to convince herself she is thirty years old, living alone, and not that little girl listening through a door.

She speaks about her mother with tenderness and anger braided tightly together. She speaks about her father mostly in fragments. What stays with her most is not only the violence itself, but the long years of pretending it was normal. Even now she minimizes her own distress automatically, then catches herself. She says she is tired of feeling ambushed by ordinary life—by raised voices, by footsteps in the hall, by the sound of glass shattering at work. She wants, more than anything, to believe in calm when it is actually there.
